# 2 Chronicles 11 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

This chapter is largely unique to Chronicles (the parallel material in vv. 1–4 appears in 1 Kings 12:21–24, but vv. 5–23 are new). It describes three aspects of Rehoboam’s early reign after the secession of the ten tribes: (1) his obedience to a prophetic prohibition against civil war; (2) his defensive fortifications; (3) the migration of faithful priests, Levites, and laity from the northern kingdom to Judah, which spiritually strengthened the southern kingdom. The chapter closes with details of Rehoboam’s family.

**Sources used:** Enduring Word (David Guzik, broadly evangelical/charismatic); Matthew Henry (non-conformist evangelical); Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (Reformed-leaning); Ellicott (Anglican); Gill (Reformed Baptist); Pulpit Commentary; Preacher’s Complete Homiletical; Precept Austin (compilation); Dr. Constable (Dispensational).

---

## Verses 1–4: Civil War Prevented by a Prophet

**v. 1: “When Rehoboam arrived in Jerusalem, he mobilized the house of Judah and Benjamin—180,000 chosen warriors—to fight against Israel and restore the kingdom to Rehoboam.”**

- This is Rehoboam’s immediate, revengeful reaction after the ten tribes revolted at Shechem (ch. 10). Judah was his own tribe; Benjamin was the tribe where Jerusalem stood, which helps explain why Benjamin stuck with him. (Matthew Henry — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/11.htm)
- The number 180,000 is about one-third of Judah’s fighting-age men under Joab’s census (2 Sam 24:9). (Preacher’s Complete Homiletical — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-11.html)
- Rehoboam intended to crush the rebellion by force. The Chronicler presents this as Rehoboam trying to counter God’s declared judgment by military might. (Precept Austin — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-11-commentary)

**v. 2: “But the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah the man of God:”**

- “But” marks a crucial contrast: before Rehoboam could act, God interrupted. Shemaiah (“heard by Jehovah”) is otherwise an obscure prophet, but he appears at two critical moments in Rehoboam’s reign (see also 2 Chr 12:5–7). (Precept Austin — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-11-commentary)
- Spurgeon commented on Shemaiah: “He appears once in this history, and then he vanishes… only fancy this one man constraining to peace a hundred and eighty thousand chosen men… by giving to them in very plain, unpolished words, the simple command of God.” (Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/ ; Precept Austin — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-11-commentary)

**v. 3: “Tell Rehoboam son of Solomon king of Judah and all the Israelites in Judah and Benjamin”**

- The phrase “king of Judah” already acknowledges the division as a fait accompli. God addresses “all Israel in Judah and Benjamin” — the Chronicler’s way of saying that the true “Israel” is now those who remain loyal to the Davidic king and the Jerusalem temple. (Ellicott — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/11.htm ; Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-11.html)

**v. 4: “that this is what the LORD says: ‘You are not to go up and fight against your brothers. Each of you must return home, for this word is from Me.’ So they listened to the words of the LORD and turned back from going against Jeroboam.”**

- God calls the northern tribes “your brothers” — a crucial reminder. Despite the political rupture, the family bond remained. (Precept Austin, citing Iain Duguid — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-11-commentary)
- “This thing is from Me” (KJV “done of me”) does not mean God authored the sinful rebellion; rather, God permitted and overruled the revolt as chastisement on the house of David for Solomon’s apostasy. The biblical writers often speak of what God permits as what God “does,” since He is ultimately sovereign. (Walter Kaiser, cited at Precept Austin — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-11-commentary)
- Rehoboam’s compliance is striking. Matthew Henry notes he either “reverenced the divine authority or… knew that he should not prosper if he should go contrary to God’s command.” (Matthew Henry — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/11.htm)
- Gill adds that Rehoboam, although forbidden to act offensively, was not forbidden to act defensively — hence the fortification work that follows. (Gill — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/11.htm)

---

## Verses 5–12: Rehoboam Fortifies Cities for Defense

**v. 5: “Rehoboam continued to live in Jerusalem, and he built up cities for defense in Judah.”**

- “Built” here means rebuilt, enlarged, and fortified existing cities; they were not newly founded. Solomon’s peaceful reign had left many of these cities neglected for defence. (Gill — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/11.htm ; JFB — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/11.htm)
- Matthew Henry notes practical wisdom: “Because God forbade him to fight, he did not therefore sit down sullenly… Those that may not be conquerors, yet may be builders.” (Matthew Henry — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/11.htm)

**vv. 6–10: The fifteen fortified cities listed — Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa, Beth-zur, Soco, Adullam, Gath, Mareshah, Ziph, Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah, Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron.**

- All fifteen lay south and west of Jerusalem, suggesting Rehoboam feared attack from Egypt (which came in ch. 12 under Shishak) rather than from the northern kingdom. (Pulpit Commentary via Precept Austin — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-11-commentary ; Enduring Word, citing Payne — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/)
- Zorah and Aijalon were originally Danite cities (Josh 19:41), but were apparently later occupied by Benjamin, hence why they are described as “in Judah and Benjamin.” (Pulpit Commentary — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/11-11.html)
- Gath was a Philistine city that had been subject to Solomon. (JFB — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/11.htm)

**v. 11: “He strengthened their fortresses and put officers in them, with supplies of food, oil, and wine.”**

- “Strengthened” (Hebrew *chazaq*) means he put the strongholds into an efficient condition for defence, appointing commandants (*negidim*, “leaders/princes”) and provisioning them. (Ellicott — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/11.htm ; Pulpit Commentary — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/11-11.html)
- Clarke notes: “In these places he laid up stores of provisions, not only to enable them to endure a siege; but also that they might be able, from their situation, to supply desolate places.” (Enduring Word, citing Clarke — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/)

**v. 12: “He also put shields and spears in all the cities and strengthened them greatly. So Judah and Benjamin belonged to him.”**

- The final clause (“Judah and Benjamin belonged to him”) mirrors the statement in 2 Chronicles 10:19 that “Israel has been in rebellion against the house of David.” This concludes the section about what Rehoboam did to consolidate his diminished kingdom. (Pulpit Commentary — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/11-11.html)
- Guzik notes that while Rehoboam succeeded in physical fortification, “overall he neglected the spiritual things necessary to strengthen his kingdom.” (Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/)

---

## Verses 13–17: The Priests, Levites, and Godly Remnant Migrate South

**v. 13: “Moreover, the priests and Levites from all their districts throughout Israel stood with Rehoboam.”**

- This was a mass defection of religious personnel from Jeroboam’s northern kingdom. They took their stand with Rehoboam because Jeroboam had instituted state-sponsored idolatry (1 Kings 12:26–33). (Enduring Word, citing Poole — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/)
- JFB calls this “an accession of moral power,” noting that “the maintenance of the true religion is the best support and safeguard of any nation.” (JFB — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/11.htm)

**v. 14: “For the Levites left their pasturelands and their possessions and went to Judah and Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his sons had rejected them as priests of the LORD.”**

- The Levites had been granted cities with pasturelands (suburbs) in each tribal allotment (Num 35:1–8). They abandoned these secure provisions to serve God freely in Jerusalem. (Matthew Henry — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/11.htm)
- Jeroboam “cast them off” — he would not allow the legitimate priests to instruct and lead the people because they would not compromise with his calf-worship. Matthew Henry adds: “No marvel if he that cast off God cast off his ministers.” (Matthew Henry — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/11.htm)
- The phrase “Jeroboam and his sons” indicates this policy continued beyond Jeroboam into the reigns of his successors. (Enduring Word, citing Payne — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/)
- Knapp remarked that as a stroke of policy, this ejection was a blunder: the Levites went over “in a body, almost, to Jeroboam’s rival, and thereby ‘strengthened the kingdom of Judah.’” (Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/)

**v. 15: “And Jeroboam appointed his own priests for the high places and for the goat demons and calf idols he had made.”**

- The Hebrew word for “goat demons” is *se‘irim* (lit. “hairy ones” or “he-goats”). This term, used also in Leviticus 17:7, refers to demonic entities associated with pagan fertility cults. JFB notes it was “applied distinctively to the goat deities, which were probably worshipped chiefly in the northern parts of his kingdom, where the heathen Canaanites still abounded.” (JFB — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/11.htm ; biblehub.com Hebrew notes — https://biblehub.com/2_chronicles/11-15.htm)
- Gill says: “idols of whatsoever kind are so called; for whosoever worships them worships not God, but devils” (cf. 1 Cor 10:20–21). (Gill — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/11.htm)
- The “calves” refer to the golden calves set up at Dan and Bethel (1 Kings 12:28), likely patterned after Egyptian bull-gods Apis and Mnevis, which Jeroboam had seen during his exile in Egypt. (JFB — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/11.htm)
- Jeroboam “ordained priests from every class of people, who were not Levites” (1 Kings 12:31). The requirements were minimal — “any who brought a bullock and seven rams” could be consecrated (2 Chr 13:9). (JFB — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/11.htm)
- Poole distinguishes two kinds of Jeroboam’s high places: some for Baal (pagan gods), others ostensibly for the true God whom he pretended to worship through the calves. (Enduring Word, citing Poole — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/)
- **Tradition note — Pentecostal/Charismatic view (Enduring Word/Guzik):** Notes that 1 Corinthians 10:20 directly connects idol-worship with demons, affirming the spiritual reality behind these entities, not merely superstition. (Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/)

**v. 16: “Those from every tribe of Israel who had set their hearts to seek the LORD their God followed the Levites to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their fathers.”**

- The migration was not limited to clergy. Lay Israelites from *all* the northern tribes who were spiritually serious (“set their hearts to seek the LORD”) also came south. This meant every tribe was represented in the southern kingdom — the Chronicler’s “all Israel” concept. (Enduring Word, citing Selman — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/)
- Matthew Henry emphasizes the priority of religious commitment over material security: “That is best for us which is best for our souls; and, in all our choices, advantages for religion must take place of all outward conveniences.” (Matthew Henry — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/11.htm)
- G. Campbell Morgan called this “a remnant of loyal souls” whose exodus was sacrificial but became a means of deliverance. (Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/)

**v. 17: “So they strengthened the kingdom of Judah and supported Rehoboam son of Solomon for three years, because they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon.”**

- “They” refers first and foremost to the godly migrants. Matthew Henry says they strengthened Judah “not only by the addition of so many persons to it… but by their piety and their prayers they procured a blessing upon the kingdom which was a sanctuary to them.” (Matthew Henry — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/11.htm)
- “Walked in the way of David and Solomon” means they served Yahweh according to the worship system those kings established. The Chronicler here ignores Solomon’s late-life apostasy and focuses on his positive legacy. (Ellicott — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/11.htm)
- The three-year limit is sobering. After three years, Rehoboam forsook the law of the LORD (2 Chr 12:1), and the strength provided by the godly influx was squandered. Gill suggests Solomon’s repentance in old age (see Ecclesiastes) may be hinted at in the phrase “the way of… Solomon.” (Gill — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/11.htm)
- Constable notes: “The faithfulness of these northern Yahweh worshippers lasted only three years, however. Rehoboam, like Solomon, was not entirely faithful.” (Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-11.html)

---

## Verses 18–23: Rehoboam’s Wives and Family

**v. 18: “And Rehoboam married Mahalath, who was the daughter of David’s son Jerimoth and of Abihail, the daughter of Jesse’s son Eliab.”**

- Jerimoth is not listed among David’s legitimate sons (1 Chr 3:1–9), so he was likely the son of a concubine. Abihail, the mother, was the daughter of Eliab (David’s eldest brother), so Mahalath was a cousin of Rehoboam. (JFB — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/11.htm ; Preacher’s Homiletical — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-11.html)
- Giving both the father’s and mother’s names for Mahalath is unusual; it may indicate the Chronicler’s interest in her Davidic lineage. (Ellicott — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/11.htm)

**v. 19: “She bore sons to him: Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham.”**

- These three sons are not mentioned elsewhere in Scripture.

**v. 20: “After her, he married Maacah daughter of Absalom, and she bore to him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith.”**

- “Daughter of Absalom” means granddaughter — Absalom’s daughter Tamar was probably her mother (2 Sam 14:27; Josephus). (JFB — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/11.htm ; Preacher’s Homiletical — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-11.html)
- Maacah becomes the mother of Abijah, who succeeds Rehoboam as king (2 Chr 12:16; 13:1–2). She remains influential into the reign of her grandson Asa, who eventually removes her from her position as queen mother because of her idolatry (1 Kings 15:13; 2 Chr 15:16).

**v. 21: “Rehoboam loved Maacah daughter of Absalom more than all his wives and concubines. In all, he had eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and he was the father of twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters.”**

- Rehoboam’s harem, though smaller than Solomon’s 700 wives and 300 concubines (1 Kings 11:3), still violated Deuteronomy 17:17, which forbade kings from multiplying wives. Guzik comments: “Rehoboam obviously did not learn from his father Solomon’s error.” (Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/)
- G. Campbell Morgan remarks that “even in the years of peace and prosperity, the animal nature came out in the multiplicity of wives and concubines.” (Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/)
- However, Matthew Henry notes an important distinction: unlike Solomon, Rehoboam does not appear to have married foreign wives. The wives listed are all from the family of David — daughters of Israel. (Matthew Henry — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/11.htm)

**v. 22: “Rehoboam appointed Abijah son of Maacah as chief prince among his brothers, intending to make him king.”**

- Abijah was not the firstborn, but Rehoboam favoured him because of his love for Maacah. Clarke says: “As he loved Maachah more than any of his wives, so he preferred her son, probably through his mother’s influence.” (Enduring Word, citing Clarke — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/)
- JFB notes that in destining a younger son for the throne without divine warrant, Rehoboam acted in violation of Deuteronomy 21:15, which forbade preferring the son of a loved wife over the firstborn son of an unloved wife. (JFB — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/11.htm)

**v. 23: “Rehoboam also acted wisely by dispersing some of his sons throughout the districts of Judah and Benjamin, and to all the fortified cities. He gave them abundant provisions and sought many wives for them.”**

- “Dealt wisely” (Hebrew root used in Exodus 1:10 of Pharaoh’s shrewd dealing) means Rehoboam acted with political calculation. By giving his many sons independent positions as governors of fortified cities, he (a) kept them occupied and content, (b) prevented them from forming a coalition against his chosen heir Abijah, and (c) placed trusted family members in key defensive positions. (Ellicott — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/11.htm ; JFB — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/11.htm)
- Gill offers an alternative reading: “he made his son Abijah to understand” — i.e., Rehoboam carefully educated Abijah in the art of government. But Gill himself prefers the standard reading: Rehoboam dispersed his sons. (Gill — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/11.htm)
- JFB compares this to Eastern royal practice: in Persia and Turkey, younger princes were historically shut in the harem or blinded/killed when a brother ascended the throne. Rehoboam’s approach of dispersing them with positions and provisions was more humane and politically astute. (JFB — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/11.htm ; Preacher’s Homiletical — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/2-chronicles-11.html)
- The giving of “many wives” to the sons may have been designed to tie each prince to the locale where he governed through marriage alliances. (JFB — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/11.htm)

---

## Denominational Distinctives and Other Views

**Reformed / Presbyterian:** The JFB commentary (Reformed-leaning) emphasizes divine sovereignty in the division of the kingdom (“this thing is done of me”) and treats Rehoboam’s obedience as an instance of God’s restraining grace. It also notes Rehoboam’s violation of Deuteronomy 17:17 and 21:15, applying covenant-law standards to evaluate the king. (JFB — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_chronicles/11.htm)

**Baptist:** Gill (Reformed Baptist) gives detailed attention to the Hebrew text and cross-references. On v. 15, he identifies the “devils” as actual demons behind idol-worship, citing 1 Cor 10:20–21. On v. 23, he considers that the “many wives” sought may have been for Abijah rather than Rehoboam himself. (Gill — https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/11.htm)

**Anglican:** Ellicott’s commentary notes the Chronicler’s unique vocabulary (“fenced cities” = ‘arê metsûrôth, a phrase peculiar to Chronicles) and observes that the Chronicler strategically ignores Solomon’s late-life idolatry when referring to “the way of David and Solomon.” (Ellicott — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/11.htm)

**Dispensational:** Constable sees in this chapter the theme that “the true Israel was now in Judah,” with the faithful from all tribes migrating south. He also notes the Chronicler’s pattern: building, defection of the faithful, and large family — all motifs demonstrating “God’s reward for faithfulness.” (Constable — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-11.html)

**Catholic and Orthodox views:** Searches on newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org could not be completed within the search limits. No distinct Catholic or Orthodox reading was identified from the available source set.

**Modern scholarship:** Searches on bibleodyssey.org and netbible.org could not be completed within the search limits. The Pulpit Commentary (1880) and Keil & Delitzsch (cited in Pulpit) do reflect 19th-century critical scholarship that notes geographical and textual details (e.g., Berth’s observation that the placement of the fifteen cities indicates fear of Egypt rather than Israel). (Pulpit Commentary — https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-chronicles/11-11.html)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic:** Enduring Word (David Guzik) treats the “goat demons” (v. 15) as real spiritual entities, not mere superstition, connecting them to 1 Corinthians 10:20 and affirming ongoing spiritual warfare realities. Guzik also gives significant attention to the prophetic power of Shemaiah’s simple obedience as a model for Spirit-empowered ministry. (Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-11/)
